Walter Russell · The Universal One (1926) · The Genero-Radiative Concept (1930)

What Russell Saw

A painter who looked at the universe as one motion, divided into two, and drew what he saw a generation before physics could measure it.

Jeromie Beasley

Walter Russell (1871–1963) was a painter and sculptor who came to physics and chemistry by way of his own vision rather than by schooling. In 1926 he printed The Universal One, and in 1930 he set out The Genero-Radiative Concept. Both books describe a single substance whose every change is a pair of opposed motions that sum to one constant. Physics of his day largely set the books aside. Read slowly, a century later and against what has since been measured, they show something more interesting than a crank's cosmology. They show a visual thinker who kept arriving at real structures by the wrong road: the oscillator's two stores, the stress in a line of force, the spiral orbit, the clock slowed by gravity, the element built from lighter ones. This paper follows his thread from the pendulum to the edge of a black hole. It shows where the thread is true, where it crosses itself, and why, for 1926, he was close.

I · One substance, two swings

The cosmic pendulum

Russell's first axiom is that there is one thing, and every difference we see is that one thing in motion. Each motion comes as a pair of opposites, and the pair always adds up to the same amount.

“the amount of energy expended in any two opposite swings of the cosmic pendulum is always quantitatively constant. The apparent variation is in the dimension of the two opposing swings”The Universal One, p.15

This is the law of an oscillator, stated by a man who had watched pendulums rather than solved for them. A swinging mass carries one fixed energy in two stores. At the ends of the swing it is all in position; at the bottom it is all in motion. The total never changes while the share moves back and forth.

E = ½ m v² + ½ k x² = constant
At the turning points v = 0, so all of E is in the spring or the height. At the centre x = 0, so all of E is in the motion. Differentiate: dE/dt = v (m dv/dt + k x) = 0, because m dv/dt = −k x is the force law. Nothing is lost; the store changes hands.
stored in positionstored in motionthe constant sum

He called the bottom of the swing a dead centre: the place where the force is zero and the mass is carried across by its own momentum. He saw the same exchange in electricity:

“At one of these dead center positions electricity changes its costume … and comes back … with all the attributes of magnetism. It is the same force exactly.”Genero-Radiative Concept, p.14

In a circuit of a coil and a capacitor that is literally what happens. The energy sits in the electric field of the capacitor, flows through the current into the magnetic field of the coil, and comes back, twice every cycle. On average the two stores hold equal shares. Russell named the two stores generation and radiation and made the whole universe of them.

He also stated the second law in the same picture: work is only ever drawn from a difference, and every difference runs down toward balance.

“Whenever one equilibrium pressure is divided into two opposing pressures, each one of the two tries to destroy the other in order that they may each return to the stability of an equilibrium.”Genero-Radiative Concept, p.11
II · Sightings

What he saw before it was measured

Russell's best results are not calculations. They are generalizations from looking hard at nature, written down before the instruments that would confirm them existed or before the theory that would explain them was accepted. Each card gives his words, his page, and what is now known.

1926 · thirteen years before Bethe

The Sun makes its own light

“The modern concept that solar energy is due to contraction is a misconcept. The energy given off from the sun is energy that is being generated within the sun.”UO p.32

Contraction could power the Sun for only about thirty million years. Nuclear fusion in the core was proposed by Eddington in 1920 and worked out by Bethe in 1939.

1926 · thirty-one years before B²FH

Heavy elements are grown

“Radium was once hydrogen; gold was lithium; man was helium; the mountain was silicon”UO p.66

Every element heavier than lithium was built from lighter ones inside stars and their explosions (Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler and Hoyle, 1957). Much of the gold in a ring was forged when neutron stars collided, as the 2017 merger GW170817 showed. His particular lineages are poetry; the principle is right.

Stars form, shine and scatter

The temperature cycle

“Cold generates. Generation contracts. Contraction integrates. Integration heats. Heat radiates. Radiation expands. Expansion disintegrates. Disintegration cools.”UO p.32

This is the life of a star-forming cloud. A cold cloud collapses under its own weight (Jeans), heats as it contracts (the virial theorem), shines, blows its gas back out with radiation and winds, and the expanding gas cools to begin again.

The Sun's equator runs ahead

Differential rotation

“the expanded magnetic bases of the equatorial belt of the sun moves faster than the contracted polar”UO p.104

The Sun's equator turns once in about 25 days, its poles in about 35 (Carrington, 1863). He also described spots drifting toward the equator through each eleven-year cycle, with opposite whirl in the two hemispheres (Spörer; Hale, 1919).

A prediction for Voyager

Moons that keep one face

“The earth's satellite, and in all probability two to four of Jupiter's … keep their same faces”UO p.226

All four large moons of Jupiter are tidally locked, as Voyager confirmed in 1979. He also named the cause: “Each acts as a brake upon the wheels of the other until they gradually meld in rigidity” (UO p.191).

A rule of the solar system

The eight-degree band

“the area of plane expansion of the ecliptic for major masses within the system is approximately eight degrees on either side of the solar equatorial plane … Beyond this area only those very much smaller masses, such as asteroids and comets are permitted”UO p.238

Every planet's orbit tilts between 3.4° and 7.2° from the Sun's equator. Only small bodies stray far: Pallas at 35°, Pluto at 17°, the comets anywhere.

Tails that lead

Comets pushed by the Sun

comets “leave vast trails of ionized material in their wake or push them ahead of them according to whether their direction is toward or away from the sun”UO p.244

A comet's ion tail points away from the Sun, so it trails on the way in and leads on the way out. The push is the solar wind and sunlight itself.

Found by spacecraft

The charged sunlit face

the planet's “positive charge is always preponderant in that part which is nearest … the sun. Also is its negative discharge always dominant in the portion farthest”UO p.78

On an airless body this is exactly so. Sunlight knocks electrons off the Moon's day side, leaving it several volts positive, while the night side charges to minus a hundred volts or more (Lunar Prospector, ARTEMIS).

Uranus on its side

A tipped-over planet

“Planets never cease turning in the same direction. They but change their positions in relation to us as observers. … We look almost directly at the south pole of Uranus”UO p.228

Uranus is tilted 97.8°. Its apparently backward spin and moons are a normal system knocked onto its side, which is his reading exactly.

The skater's law

Contraction spins up

“Decrease of volume is exactly balanced by acceleration of revolution. Equal areas must be covered in contracted orbits as in expanded orbits of equal mass.”UO p.146

Conservation of angular momentum: Kepler's equal areas, the spinning skater, the collapsing star that becomes a millisecond pulsar.

Two bodies, one pivot

The point both bodies swing around

“One of these is the mutual gravitative center around which both masses swing.”GRC p.20

Earth and Moon both orbit their common centre of mass, 4,670 km from the Earth's centre and so inside the Earth. His chart on the next page draws it just inside the surface.

The compass at the equator

The dip equator

“the compass needle loses its dip on the zero isoclinal line which roughly follows the geographic equator”UO pp.104–106

A freely hung needle lies level on the magnetic equator and tips the other way on crossing it, north end down in the north and up in the south.

III · Streams that join, streams that part

Opposed and parallel flows

The idea Russell returns to more than any other is that two flows running the same way pull together, and two flows running against each other push apart. He explained a compass needle with water pipes:

“Just as the two separate streams of water would apparently repel each other if the pipes were so joined, so would they appear to attract each other and flow as one stream if the pipes were joined so that their streams were flowing in the same direction.”The Universal One, p.171
“Electricity … tends to shorten a line in the direction of its length.”Genero-Radiative Concept, p.8

This is the picture Faraday drew and Maxwell made exact. A line of magnetic force behaves like a stretched elastic cord that also swells sideways: it pulls along its own length and pushes on its neighbours. Two wires carrying current the same way share lines that wrap around both, and those lines, trying to shorten, draw the wires together. Two wires carrying current in opposite ways have their lines crowded into the gap between them, and the crowding pushes them apart. Parallel flows attract; opposed flows expand. Russell had the rule and the right image for it.

field linesmagnetic pressure B²/2μ₀force on each wire
Slide from +1 A through zero to −1 A and watch the lines change from wrapping both wires, to circling one, to crowding apart.
Right-hand current—
Force per metre—
Separation—
The wires—

The lines drawn are exact, and they are recomputed each time you move the slider. Each is a curve along which the flux function ψ = I₁ ln r₁ + I₂ ln r₂ is constant, where r₁ and r₂ are the distances to the two wires. With both currents the same way, ψ = ln(r₁r₂) and the lines are Cassini ovals: close in, each wire has its own loops; farther out, the lines pass around both wires at once. With the currents opposed, ψ = ln(r₁/r₂) and the lines are circles of Apollonius, each one around a single wire, packed tight in the gap. The blue glow is the magnetic pressure, brightest where the lines crowd. Press Let the wires move and the stress does its work: the wires close together, or fly apart.

Along a line of force: tension B²/2μ₀ per unit area (the line pulls)
Across a line of force: pressure B²/2μ₀ per unit area (the line pushes)
Both come from Maxwell's stress tensor, Tij = (BiBj − ½δijB²)/μ₀. Along the field the two terms give B² − ½B² = +½B², a pull. Across it only −½B² is left, a push. One tensor gives both behaviours.
Force per metre between two long wires: F/ℓ = μ₀ I₁ I₂ / (2π d)
It is attractive when I₁ and I₂ run the same way and repulsive when they run opposite. For one ampere in each at one metre it is exactly 2 × 10⁻⁷ newton per metre. From 1948 to 2019 this number was the international definition of the ampere.

The same stress holds a larger lesson that Russell reached for and did not finish. Anything that holds itself together must balance its pushes against its pulls. Summed over the whole object, the outward pressure must equal the inward tension exactly (von Laue, 1911; the virial theorem). A magnetic field by itself always nets outward. A star shines because its hot gas pushes out and its gravity pulls in, and the two lock at 2K + U = 0, twice the thermal energy against the gravitational energy. A nucleus holds while the pull of the strong force beats the electric push of its protons. It splits when the push wins, which is why the heaviest nuclei fission. Russell kept the pushes of his cosmos (radiation, expansion, pressure), and for the pull he reached for buoyancy. That choice runs through everything in section VIII.

IV · The spiral

“All orbits are spiral”

“All orbits are spiral.”The Universal One, p.118

Russell gave laws for the planets: orbital speed falls as the inverse of distance, and the period grows as the square of the distance. Measured against the solar system these are wrong; the true laws are Kepler's. Taken together, though, they are not random. They describe one consistent world, and the way to see it is Newton's own scaling argument.

Suppose the potential energy grows as a power of distance, U ∝ rn.
Stretch every length by λ and every time by τ. Accelerations change by λ/τ²; forces from U change by λn−1.
The motion is still a solution when λ/τ² = λn−1, that is τ = λ1−n/2, and speeds scale as λ/τ = λn/2.
Newton's gravity has n = −1: periods scale as a3/2 (Kepler's third law) and speeds as a−1/2.
Russell's speed law v ∝ a−1 needs n/2 = −1, so n = −2. Then τ ∝ a², which is his period law.
His two laws agree with each other exactly. They describe a world whose force falls as 1/r³.

What does an orbit do in that world? Newton answered it in the Principia (Book I, Proposition 45). Take a nearly circular orbit and ask how far it turns before its far point comes back.

Write u = 1/r. For a force k/rp, the orbit obeys u″ + u = (mk/L²) up−2, where L is the angular momentum and ″ is the second derivative with respect to angle.
A circle is u = u₀ with u₀ = (mk/L²) u₀p−2. Nudge it: u = u₀ + δ.
To first order δ″ + δ = (p − 2) δ, so δ″ + (3 − p) δ = 0.
The wobble repeats every 2π/√(3 − p) of angle, so the far point returns after ψ = π/√(3 − p).
Newton, p = 2: ψ = π, half a turn, and the ellipse closes. Russell, p = 3: ψ is infinite. The orbit never comes back. A nudged circle unwinds into a spiral, inward or outward (Cotes, 1722).

So Russell's orbital laws describe the world where every orbit is a spiral. That world exists. Einstein's gravity contains it, at one exact distance from every compact mass.

In general relativity the orbit equation gains one term: u″ + u = GM/L² + (3GM/c²) u².
Nudge a circle again: δ″ + (1 − 6GM u₀/c²) δ = 0. Compare with δ″ + (3 − p) δ = 0:
p = 2 + 6GM/(c² r)
Far away p is 2 and Newton holds. At Mercury p − 2 is 1.6 × 10⁻⁷, which shifts its far point by 43 seconds of arc per century, the effect Einstein explained in 1915. At r = 6GM/c², p reaches 3 exactly. That is the innermost stable circular orbit: inside it, every orbit spirals. For the Sun's mass it lies 8.9 km from the centre; for a neutron star of 1.4 solar masses, 12.4 km, close to the star's own surface.

In units of GM/c². For the Sun that unit is 1.48 km; Mercury orbits at 39 million of them.

V · Beyond the horizon

His lines, where they come true

Russell wrote about the cosmos as though gravity were everywhere as strong as it is near a collapsed star. Taken at the Sun's distance, most of his strong statements fail. Taken near a black hole, several of them read like field notes. Each line is his; beside it is general relativity at the scale where the line becomes true, with the number computed for this paper.

“All orbits are spiral.”UO p.118

Inside 6 GM/c² no circular orbit is stable. Gas at the inner edge of every black-hole disk spirals in.

p = 2 + 6GM/(c²r) = 3 at r = 6 GM/c²

“'light rays' do not proceed directly from the sun to a planet in straight lines. They follow the orbital lines … exactly as does this planet.”UO p.84

At 3 GM/c² light itself travels in a circle, the photon sphere. Light sent sideways just outside it winds around the hole before it escapes.

released 0.0001 GM/c² outside: 1.83 turns, then escapes

“No mass can remain fixed in position, not even that which has been apparently arrested in its motion.”UO p.142

Inside the ergosphere of a spinning hole, nothing can stand still. Every body and every ray of light is swept around with the spin.

spin 0.9, r = 1.9 GM/c²: slowest allowed turning +0.030 c³/GM

“The vortex of any system is always luminous.”UO p.198

Matter spiralling down to the innermost stable orbit turns part of its rest mass into light before it falls. This is why quasar centres outshine their galaxies.

5.7% of rest-mass energy (no spin); 42.3% (maximal spin)

“Time itself is an effect of gravitation”UO p.34

Clocks near a compact mass run slow, and outgoing light near the horizon barely moves as seen from far away.

at 2.001 GM/c²: clock rate 0.022; outgoing light 0.0005 c

“That which is generated must be radiated.”UO p.31

Even a black hole radiates. Hawking showed in 1974 that a horizon glows at a temperature set by its mass.

one solar mass: 6.2 × 10⁻⁸ K

Turned around
“Its minimum of generative pressure is exerted from its equatorial plane and its maximum pressure from its pole.”UO p.106

Real black holes feed through a disk in the equatorial plane and throw matter out in jets along the poles. He had the two flows and the two directions, and set them the other way round.

VI · The second dial is time

The spirals are real. They take a lifetime.

Far from a black hole Russell's spirals still happen, only slowly. He wrote that the planets are “Slowly expanding, they are drawing away from the sun, assisted by the sun in their recession” (UO p.144). The Sun loses about 5.8 billion kilograms a second to light and wind. With less mass holding them, every orbit widens.

With angular momentum fixed and a slowly shrinking mass, a·M stays constant, so da/dt = −a (dM/dt)/M.
dM/dt ÷ M = 5.76 × 10⁹ kg/s × 3.156 × 10⁷ s/yr ÷ 1.989 × 10³⁰ kg = 9.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ per year. At one astronomical unit this gives 1.37 cm per year. By the time the Sun becomes a white dwarf of 0.54 solar masses, every planetary orbit will have grown by a factor of 1.85.
—
VII · The octave

The elements as music

Russell read the periodic table as a sequence of musical octaves. Each octave rises through four tones to a crest at carbon, falls through four more, and rests at the inert gas. He printed it as a formula:

“4±3+2+1+0−1−2−3−4±”The Universal One, p.38

His wave and the chemistry. Along the bottom, the second period of the table, lithium to neon. The red and blue curve is Russell's octave: charge rising +1, +2, +3 to carbon's ±4, then −3, −2, −1 and the rest at zero. The gold bars are the ordinary combining powers of these elements (Abegg, 1904): 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. Point for point, the size of his tones is the valence.

Where chemistry really is symmetric about the middle of a period, the octave works. It gives the valences. It reproduces the pattern of hydride formulas: LiH, BeH₂, BH₃, CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, HF. It tracks the rise and fall of atomic volume and melting point across a period. His numbering (octave = period + 3) places the start of the transition metals in his seventh octave, which is the fourth period, where they begin. His empty slots called for undiscovered elements after neodymium, between tungsten and osmium, and after polonium. Promethium (1945), rhenium (1925) and astatine (1940) filled them.

Where chemistry is not symmetric, the octave forces it to be. He gave each side of the ninth octave thirteen places, while nature fills fourteen (the f-block) and ten (the d-block). The forced symmetry left two empty places between lutetium and tantalum, where only hafnium exists, and one between platinum and gold, where there is none. To keep atomic mass rising smoothly, his table printed argon at 39.09 and nickel at 59, turning back two known mass inversions.

VIII · Where the thread crossed

How the vision went wrong, and why

Russell's errors are not scattered. Nearly all come from three habits, and each habit is the misuse of something true.

The two columns

He kept every pair of opposites in two long parallel columns and treated any two items in the same column as the same thing.

Generation
Radiation
contraction
expansion
gravity, attraction
repulsion
electricity
magnetism
heat
cold
red
blue

Gravity attracts, so electricity, sitting in the same column, must attract its like. That is how he came to write that “the commonly accepted law that like charges repel and opposite charges attract is an inconsistent and flagrant error” (GRC p.4), and that magnetism is a repulsion. Gravity really does pull like toward like. Electricity and magnetism each push and pull. His water-pipe picture of section III was right about flows; filing electricity beside gravity was not.

The rigid wheel carried into the sky

For a rigid body he was exact: the Earth's surface turns at about 1,000 miles an hour, 750 a thousand miles down, 500 at two thousand, 250 at three thousand (UO p.216), falling in a straight line to the centre. He carried the laws of a solid wheel to free orbits. That produced his planet laws, and those laws in turn made him reject the masses he himself quoted: “Jupiter is, roughly, only double the mass of the earth, and Mercury's mass actually exceeds that of the earth” (UO p.192). Kepler's law applied to each planet's moons gives Jupiter 317.8 Earth masses and Mercury 0.055, the textbook figures he printed and then overruled.

Buoyancy in place of the pull

He held that every mass floats at the level matching its density, like a cork in water: “There is a true position for every potential” (UO p.143). For a planet that keeps its angular momentum this is half right. The balance of gravity against the spin term makes a genuine valley in the energy, and a planet pushed from it oscillates about it. With the angular momentum dropped, the picture fails: “The present theory that the moon would fall to the earth if it were not sustained by its motion is a mistaken one” (UO p.144). Stopped in its path, the Moon would fall to Earth in about 4.8 days. This is the missing pull of section III.

IX · His charts, redrawn

Seven charts from the books, and what they show now

Russell was an illustrator before he was anything else, and the books carry him in their charts more than their prose. Here are seven of the best, from the original printings. Beside each is the same idea drawn again with what is now known. Everything he drew correctly is kept, and each correction is shown rather than stated.

Redrawn: the wheel is the phase portrait

Russell drew the pendulum as a wheel, and the wheel is right. Plot a swinging mass with its position across and its momentum up, and its whole history is one circle. The radius is the energy, which never changes. Going round the circle is the trade between the two stores: at the ends of the swing (left and right) all of it is in position; at the dead centre (top and bottom) all of it is in motion. What the correction removes is the tones and colours laid over the wheel. What it keeps is the circle and its constant radius.

x²/A² + p²/(mωA)² = 1 ⇔ ½kx² + p²/2m = ½kA² = E

Redrawn: a true inspiral opens as it closes

His spiral packs its turns tighter toward the centre. Two bodies that lose energy to gravitational waves do spiral together, as the Hulse–Taylor pulsars are doing now, but the turns spread apart as they go in. The orbit shrinks faster the smaller it gets while each turn takes less time, so the step from one turn to the next grows. The last turns are the widest; that is the “chirp” heard by gravitational-wave detectors. Inside 6 GM/c² the spiral stops being gradual and becomes a plunge (violet).

da/dt = −K/a³ and the period P ∝ a3/2, so the step per turn is Δa = −K′ a−3/2: larger as a shrinks.
Eccentricity e—
An orbit like this—

Redrawn: orbits are slices of a cone

He reached for a cone to explain eccentric orbits, and the cone is exactly right. Every orbit under an inverse-square force is a conic section, a slice through a cone. A level cut gives a circle, a tilted cut an ellipse, a cut parallel to the side a parabola, and a steeper cut a hyperbola. Apollonius named the curves around 200 BC; Newton proved the planets travel on them. The correction is the Sun's place. It sits at a focus of the curve (the gold point), not on the axis of any cone. The tilt that matters is not the orbit's lean against the Sun's path. It is set by the planet's speed at a given distance.

Cutting a cone of half-angle α with a plane at angle β to its axis: e = cos β / cos α
For an orbit: e² = 1 + 2EL²/(m k²), with k = GMm, E the energy and L the angular momentum

Redrawn: speed peaks at the wall, pressure falls at the heart

One panel of his is exactly right: “Orbit decreases · Revolution increases.” Air drawn inward keeps its angular momentum and spins faster, which is how a wide slow swirl becomes a violent narrow one. The rest is corrected here. The wind is fastest at the edge of the core, not at a point. The pressure is lowest at the centre, held down by the spin, and that deficit together with the updraft is what lifts heavy objects. There is no magnetic “point of north.” The curves are the Rankine vortex: solid rotation inside the core, v ∝ 1/r outside it.

Outside the core v = Γ/(2πr); inside v = Ωr; balance dp/dr = ρv²/r
Total pressure deficit at the centre = ρ vmax². At 90 m/s: 1.2 × 90² = 9,720 Pa ≈ 97 hPa, close to the 100 hPa drop measured inside the Manchester, South Dakota tornado of 2003.

Redrawn: spin sets the shape

Two of his statements hold. “The road to appearance of form … must be by the way of plane”: planets are born in flat disks of gas and dust around young stars, and spheres form inside the plane. Centrifugal effect pushes out “preponderantly from the plane of the equator”, which is why spinning bodies bulge at the equator. The correction is that flatness is not a stage of life. It is set by spin now. The chart plots each planet's measured flattening against its spin parameter q, the ratio of equatorial spin to gravity. A body of uniform density would lie on the line f = 5q/4. The giant planets lie below it because they are denser at the centre. Mars sits slightly above, because its stiff crust holds a shape that spin alone does not set.

q = ω²R³/GM; uniform body: f ≈ 5q/4 (Maclaurin); Saturn q = 0.155, f = 0.098

Redrawn: the tide is a difference of pulls

He placed a “mutual gravitative center” between Earth and Moon, just inside the Earth. That is right: both bodies circle their centre of mass, 4,670 km from the Earth's centre. He wrote that tides are not caused by the Moon's pull, and here the correction is precise. The tide is the difference of the pull across the Earth. The near side is pulled more than the centre and the far side less, so the Earth is stretched along the line to the Moon and squeezed around its waist. That makes two bulges, one on each side, and two tides a day. The arrows show the stretching field, exact in shape.

Tidal acceleration ≈ 2GMMoonR/d³ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ m/s² along the line; half as much, inward, across it. Field shape ∝ (2x, −y).

Redrawn: the octaves grow

His clock gives every octave the same eight places, which is exactly true for the second and third rows of the table (lithium to neon, sodium to argon). After that nature does something his clock could not: each new kind of orbital shell adds room. Ten transition metals open inside the fourth row, which he caught as his “mid-tones” beginning in octave seven. Fourteen lanthanides open inside the sixth. The row lengths run 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32: twice the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, each used twice.

Shell capacity 2n²: 2, 8, 18, 32. The rows take them in the order 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 (the Madelung filling rule).
X · Russell, corrected

His universe with the pull put back

Take the three habits of section VIII and repair each one. Put the missing pull back into buoyancy, let his planets' own measured speeds decide the planet laws, and sort the signs of the forces force by force. What comes out is still recognisably his universe, and it runs.

1 · “There is a true position for every potential”

the valley, Ueff(r)the planetits orbit, seen from above
Kept—
True position—

The planet starts at distance 1 with part of the sideways speed a circle would need. The gold curve is the effective potential, gravity's pull plus the outward push of its own spin: Ueff = −GMm/r + L²/(2mr²). Its lowest point, at r = L²/(GMm²), is Russell's “true position”. Keep the angular momentum and the planet rocks back and forth about that point forever, as he said a displaced Moon would, “exactly as a ball of air forced under water would rise”. Take it all away and the valley vanishes. The planet falls straight in. Our Moon, stopped dead, would reach the Earth in 4.85 days.

2 · The planet laws, decided by the planets

Both lines pass through the Earth. Russell's law, speed ∝ 1/a, falls too fast; by Neptune it predicts 0.99 km/s. Kepler's law, speed ∝ 1/√a, runs through every planet; it predicts 5.43 km/s for Neptune, and Neptune moves at 5.43.

The same law weighs the planets from their moons, and that settles his masses too:

BodyRussell (UO p.192)Weighed by orbits
Sun“vastly more than 332,000” Earths332,946
Jupiter“roughly, only double”317.9 (from Io)
Mercury“exceeds that of the earth”0.055 (spacecraft orbits)
M = 4π²a³ / (G T²). Io: a = 421,700 km, T = 1.769 days ⇒ M = 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg = 317.9 Earths.

3 · The signs of the forces, sorted

What meets whatLike with likeUnlikeRussell
Mass and mass (gravity)pull—right: gravity gathers like to like
Charge and chargepushpullreversed: he had like charges attract
Current and currentparallel flows pullopposed flows pushright: his water pipes, UO p.171

The columns of section VIII fold everything attractive into one family. Sorted force by force, gravity keeps the rule he gave it. Currents keep the rule of his water pipes, and magnets obey it too when set end to end, because the lines of force run straight through both. Charges alone run the other way.

One constant, two storesThe pendulum and its phase circle: section I and chart one.
Parallel pulls, opposed pushesThe two wires, moving under their own stress: section III.

XI · What he saw

The dance, seen clearly

Russell worked with a painter's eye, and he saw the forms: the spiral, the paired flows, the two stores of one energy, the balance that every held thing must strike. What he lacked was the pull that answers every push, and the patience to let a measured number overrule a beautiful symmetry. Put the pull back and let the numbers stand, as sections IX and X do, and a surprising share of his universe turns out to be ours: the wheel is a phase portrait, the cone holds every orbit, the streams obey Ampère, the spiral waits at six gravitational radii. For 1926, he was very close.

Evidence

This page is the interactive companion to the paper What Russell Saw (Jeromie Beasley, 2026), which gives every derivation in full, the Lean certificates, and the scripts that reproduce each number. The paper, this page and the complete code package are distributed together.

Readings, checks and sources

Both books were read three times in full from scans of the original printings: The Universal One (1926) and The Genero-Radiative Concept (1930). Every quotation here was taken verbatim from the page cited, using the printed page number. Each claim in the books was entered in a ledger with its page. Each was then graded as a formal statement, an empirical statement or a metaphysical one, and marked as holding, failing, holding in part, or having no truth value.

Computed for this paper. Near-circular orbits in Newtonian, inverse-cube and Schwarzschild gravity, integrated by Binet's equation. The apsidal angle was checked against π/√(3 − p) at p = 2, 2.5 and 2.9, and against π/√(1 − 6GM/(c²r)) to four decimals. Also computed:

  • light near the photon sphere;
  • the allowed turning rates in the equatorial plane of a Kerr hole of spin 0.9;
  • accretion efficiency at the innermost stable orbit, 1 − (1 − 2/r)/√(1 − 3/r) at r = 6;
  • clock rates √(1 − 2GM/(c²r));
  • orbit widening from solar mass loss;
  • Poynting–Robertson infall times (1,744 years for a 1 µm grain from 1 AU);
  • the Hawking temperature of one solar mass;
  • the field lines of two currents as contours of ψ = I₁ ln r₁ + k I₁ ln r₂ for any current ratio k;
  • Jupiter's mass from Io (317.9 Earths); the barycentre (4,668 km); the lunar tidal acceleration (1.10 × 10⁻⁶ m/s²); the Moon's free-fall time (4.85 days);
  • the spin parameter q = ω²R³/GM of six planets against their measured flattening. Five fall below the uniform-body line 5q/4; Mars (f = 0.00589 against 5q/4 = 0.00574) sits just above it;
  • the Rankine vortex deficit ρv²max at 90 m/s (97 hPa).

From The Genero-Radiative Concept: the Earth and Moon chart (p.21). All are photographed from the original printings.

Taken from published measurements. WASP-12b's orbital decay, about 29 ms per year, with engulfment in about 3 million years (Yee et al. 2020). The Hulse–Taylor binary pulsar, shrinking about 3.5 m per year and merging in about 300 million years. The Moon's recession, 3.8 cm per year by lunar laser ranging. Planetary masses from the orbits of their moons and spacecraft. Planetary tilts, inclinations, rotation periods, radii, GM values and flattening (NASA planetary fact sheets). Orbital speeds and eccentricities of the planets. The pressure drop inside the 2003 Manchester, South Dakota tornado.
